message.content: Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) are both mammals, but they belong to different orders—Carnivora for lions and Perissodactyla for zebras. Their most recent common ancestor is therefore a member of the larger clade **Laurasiatheria**, which includes many modern mammalian groups such as ungulates, carnivores, bats, and whales. This ancestor would have been a small, likely insectivorous mammal that lived roughly 70–80 million years ago during the late Cretaceous/early Paleogene period.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. We can provide an explanation: lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) share a common ancestor within the order Carnivora? Wait, lions are mammals, specifically within the family Felidae, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are mammals, family Equidae, suborder Perissodactyla. So their common ancestor would be at the level of the class Mammalia, but more precisely, they diverged from a common ancestor in the order Artiodactyla? Actually, lions are in the order Carnivora, while zebras are in the order Perissodactyla. Both orders belong to the clade Laurasiatheria. So the common ancestor would be a mammal from the clade Laurasiatheria, perhaps a small mammal from the late Cretaceous or early Paleogene. But we can say that the last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived around 70 million years ago, belonging to the clade Laurasiatheria.

We should give a concise answer. No tool needed.
